stages.title: Electronics Basics
stages.description: Voltage, current and resistance, Ohm's law, series and parallel resistors, and building a first LED circuit on a breadboard.
learningObjectives: Define voltage, current and resistance with their units and apply Ohm's law (V = I x R)
Calculate total resistance for resistors in series and in parallel
Explain how a solderless breadboard's strips, rails and center ravine are connected
Choose a current-limiting resistor for an LED and connect the LED with the right polarity

explainBack.question: You want to light an LED from a 5 V supply on a breadboard. Explain the quantities involved, how you size the resistor, and how you wire it so it actually works.
rubric: Voltage (volts) is the potential difference that pushes charge, current (amps) is the rate of charge flow, resistance (ohms) opposes flow, and V = I x R
In series the same current flows through each part and resistances add; in parallel each part sees the same voltage, 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ..., and the total is less than the smallest resistor

Each breadboard terminal row of five holes is connected internally, the center ravine isolates the two halves (so DIP chips can straddle it), and the side power rails run lengthwise but left and right rails are not joined unless jumpered
An LED conducts only from anode (longer leg) to cathode, and needs a series resistor R = (Vs - Vf) / I, keeping current around or below its rated ~20 mA; without one it can destroy itself

resources.title: Ohms Law Explained - The basics circuit theory
resources.description: An animated introduction to voltage, current and resistance and how Ohm's law ties them together, with worked examples.
keyPoints: Introduces voltage, current and resistance with analogies
Shows the Ohm's law triangle for solving V, I or R
Works through simple example circuits

resources.title: Voltage, Current, Resistance, and Ohm's Law
resources.description: Defines voltage, current and resistance using a water-tank analogy, derives Ohm's law and applies it to protect an LED from too much current.
keyPoints: Voltage is potential difference in volts; current is charge flow in amps; resistance is in ohms
Ohm's law: V = I x R lets you solve for any one quantity from the other two
Water analogy: pressure = voltage, flow = current, hose width = resistance
LED example picks a standard 560 ohm resistor to keep current under the LED's 18 mA limit

resources.title: Series and Parallel Circuits
resources.description: Explains what makes components series or parallel and how to combine resistors (and capacitors/inductors) in each arrangement.
keyPoints: Series parts share one node and carry the same current
Parallel parts share two nodes and have the same voltage across them
Series resistors add; parallel use 1/R_total = sum of 1/R
N equal resistors in parallel give R/N; parallel total is below the smallest resistor

resources.title: Arduino Tutorial 3: Understanding How Breadboards Work
resources.description: A hands-on lesson showing how a breadboard is wired internally and how to build a first prototype circuit on it.
keyPoints: Shows which breadboard holes are connected together
Explains the power rails and center channel
Builds a simple LED circuit on the board

resources.title: How to Use a Breadboard
resources.description: A guide to the anatomy of a solderless breadboard: terminal strips, the center ravine, power rails and how to place parts and chips.
keyPoints: Holes sit on a standard 0.1 in (2.54 mm) pitch
Each terminal-strip row has five connected clips
The center ravine isolates the two sides so DIP chips can straddle it
Side power rails run lengthwise; left and right rails are not connected to each other

resources.title: Light-Emitting Diodes (LEDs)
resources.description: Covers LED polarity, forward voltage and current ratings, and how to calculate the series resistor that keeps an LED from burning out.
keyPoints: Anode is the longer leg; current only flows anode to cathode
Each LED drops a forward voltage (about 2.4 V for the example red LED)
Current-limiting resistor: R = (Vs - Vf) / I
Typical LEDs are rated about 20 mA continuous; without a resistor the LED destroys itself

stages.title: Microcontrollers & GPIO
stages.description: How microcontroller boards like Arduino differ from single-board computers like Raspberry Pi, and how their pins handle digital, analog and PWM signals.
learningObjectives: Contrast a microcontroller board (Arduino) with a single-board computer (Raspberry Pi)
Distinguish digital from analog signals and describe logic levels
Convert an ADC reading into a voltage
Explain how PWM and duty cycle approximate an analog output

explainBack.question: A friend asks whether to use an Arduino or a Raspberry Pi to read a potentiometer and dim an LED. Explain the key differences and how the board reads the knob and dims the light.
rubric: A microcontroller such as an Arduino runs a single program with no operating system and uses very little power, while a Raspberry Pi runs a full Linux operating system
Raspberry Pi GPIO pins have no analog inputs (it needs an external ADC), whereas an Arduino Uno has six analog input pins
Digital signals take a limited set of values, usually a high level (5 V, 3.3 V or 1.8 V) and low (0 V); analog signals vary continuously
Arduino's 10-bit ADC returns 0-1023 from analogRead(), so voltage = reading / 1023 x 5 V on a 5 V board
PWM switches a digital pin rapidly; the duty cycle (percent of time high) sets the average output, and the frequency must be high enough (about 100 Hz or more for LEDs) to avoid visible flicker

resources.title: Arduino vs. Raspberry Pi - Electronics with Becky Stern | DigiKey
resources.description: Becky Stern compares Arduino microcontroller boards with Raspberry Pi single-board computers and when to choose each.
keyPoints: Contrasts microcontrollers with single-board computers
Discusses which projects suit each platform
Covers practical trade-offs such as power and complexity

resources.title: Microcomputers
resources.provider: John Abbott College (Connected Objects course notes)
resources.description: College lecture notes comparing the Raspberry Pi and Arduino: operating system, GPIO, analog inputs, power draw and languages.
keyPoints: Raspberry Pi runs a Linux OS that manages drivers, memory, networking and video
Arduino needs no operating system and is best at single tasks
Pi has 40 GPIOs but none are analog; Arduino Uno has 6 analog inputs
Pi 4 draws roughly 700+ mA at 5 V; Arduino Uno about 50 mA

resources.title: Analog vs. Digital
resources.description: Explains continuous analog signals versus discrete digital ones, with examples, logic levels, and how microcontrollers bridge the two.
keyPoints: Analog signals can take any value in a range
Digital signals use a finite set of values, usually two
High logic level is usually 5 V, 3.3 V or 1.8 V; low is usually 0 V
Microcontrollers use ADCs and DACs to work with analog signals

resources.title: Analog to Digital Conversion
resources.description: Shows how an Arduino's ADC turns a pin voltage into a number and how to convert that number back into volts.
keyPoints: Arduino's ADC is 10-bit: 1024 levels, values 0-1023
On a 5 V board, 1023 corresponds to 5 V
analogRead(A3) returns the reading for pin A3
Worked example: a reading of 334 is about 1.63 V

resources.title: Arduino Tutorial 8: Understanding Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) and the Arduino Analog Write Command
resources.description: A classroom-style lesson explaining PWM and using Arduino's analogWrite command to approximate analog voltages.
keyPoints: Explains how fast on/off switching approximates a voltage
Relates duty cycle to the average voltage
Demonstrates analogWrite on an Arduino pin

resources.title: Pulse Width Modulation
resources.description: Defines PWM, duty cycle and frequency, and shows how PWM dims LEDs, mixes RGB colors and positions hobby servos.
keyPoints: PWM is a digital signal whose high time is varied
Duty cycle is the percent of each period the signal is high (0% off, 100% fully on)
LED dimming needs about 100 Hz or faster to avoid flicker
Servos expect 1-2 ms pulses about every 20 ms

stages.title: Sensors & Actuators
stages.description: Reading resistive sensors through a voltage divider and choosing and safely driving DC, servo and stepper motors.
learningObjectives: Read a resistive sensor with a voltage divider and an analog input
Compare brushed DC motors, RC servos and stepper motors
Explain why motors need a transistor or H-bridge driver instead of a GPIO pin
Protect a circuit from motor spikes and supply noise

explainBack.question: Your robot has a light sensor, a servo for a gripper, and two DC drive motors. Explain how the microcontroller reads the sensor and how you would wire and protect the motors.
rubric: A resistive sensor (e.g. a photocell) is paired with a fixed resistor as a voltage divider, Vout = Vin x R2 / (R1 + R2), and the ADC reads Vout
A hobby RC servo gives about 180 degrees of position control using an internal potentiometer for feedback and is commanded with logic-level pulses
A stepper motor gives position control without an encoder, while a brushed DC motor has no position control unless an encoder is added
Motors draw more current than a microcontroller pin can supply, so a transistor or H-bridge driver switches them; an H-bridge can reverse current to change direction and PWM sets speed
A flyback diode across the motor gives the voltage spike at switch-off a safe path, and motors should have their own supply that shares a common ground with the logic

resources.title: Controlling DC Motors with the L298N H Bridge and Arduino
resources.description: Explains how an H-bridge driver lets a microcontroller control DC motor speed and direction, then wires an L298N module to an Arduino.
keyPoints: Explains why microcontrollers cannot drive motors directly
Shows how an H-bridge reverses motor direction
Uses PWM to control motor speed with an L298N

resources.title: Voltage Dividers
resources.description: Derives the voltage divider equation and applies it to reading resistive sensors, potentiometers and simple level shifting.
keyPoints: Vout = Vin x R2 / (R1 + R2)
Microcontrollers measure voltage, so resistive sensors are paired with a fixed resistor
Example: photocell (1-10 kohm) with 5.6 kohm gives a useful voltage swing for an ADC
Dividers should not be used to power loads

resources.title: Adafruit Motor Selection Guide
resources.description: A comparison of brushed DC, brushless, stepper and servo motors, plus motor controllers and how to power motors.
keyPoints: Brushed DC motors have no position control without an encoder
Steppers provide position control without extra feedback
RC servos give about 180 degrees of position control via a shaft potentiometer and logic-level pulses
An H-bridge is a 4-transistor circuit that reverses motor current
Motors can cause supply fluctuations that disrupt other devices on the same supply

resources.title: Arduino Lesson 13. DC Motors
resources.description: Builds a transistor-switched DC motor circuit with a protection diode and controls its speed with PWM from an Arduino.
keyPoints: A small DC motor can draw more current than an Arduino pin can handle
A transistor lets a small pin current switch the larger motor current
A diode across the motor shorts out the reverse spike when power is cut
Some motors draw 1000 mA, more than USB can supply

resources.title: Diodes
resources.description: Explains diode behavior and common uses, including the flyback diode that protects circuits from inductive voltage spikes.
keyPoints: Diodes pass current in one direction
Switching off an inductor (motor, relay) creates a large voltage spike
A flyback diode across the load gives the spike a safe path to dissipate

resources.title: Controlling DC Motors with the L298N Dual H-Bridge and an Arduino
resources.description: Written companion to the video: how H-bridges work, the L298N's voltage drop, separate motor power and common ground.
keyPoints: DC motors need more current and voltage than a microcontroller can supply
An H-bridge reverses polarity to change direction; PWM on the enable line sets speed
The L298N loses about 1.4 V internally, so supply a bit above motor voltage
Motor and logic supplies must share a common ground

stages.title: Communication Protocols
stages.description: How microcontrollers talk to sensors and other chips over UART serial, I2C and SPI, and why pull-up resistors matter.
learningObjectives: Wire and configure an asynchronous serial (UART) link
Explain I2C addressing and why the bus needs pull-up resistors
Describe SPI's signals and when to choose it over I2C
Explain floating inputs and how pull-up resistors fix them

explainBack.question: You need to connect a GPS module, three I2C sensors and a fast SPI display to one microcontroller. Explain how each bus is wired and what settings or parts each one needs.
rubric: UART is asynchronous (no clock line): both sides must use the same baud rate (e.g. 9600) and frame format (e.g. 8N1), TX connects to the other device's RX, and grounds are shared
I2C uses two shared wires, SDA (data) and SCL (clock); each device has an address (commonly 7-bit) sent in an address frame, and the addressed device acknowledges
I2C lines are open-drain and need pull-up resistors (commonly 4.7 kohm) on SDA and SCL

SPI uses a clock, two data lines (controller-out and controller-in) and a separate active-low chip-select per peripheral; it is synchronous, full-duplex, faster than I2C, but needs more wires and suits short distances
An unconnected (floating) input reads unpredictably; a pull-up resistor (about 10 kohm) holds it high until a button pulls it to ground, and Arduino's INPUT_PULLUP enables an internal one

resources.title: I2C Part 1 - Using 2 Arduinos
resources.description: Introduces the I2C bus, its two lines and addressing, then links two Arduinos over I2C using the Wire library.
keyPoints: Covers I2C history, speeds and the SDA/SCL lines
Explains addresses and pull-up resistors
Demonstrates Arduino-to-Arduino I2C with the Wire library

resources.title: Serial Communication
resources.description: Explains asynchronous serial: baud rates, framing, wiring and the difference between TTL and RS-232 voltage levels.
keyPoints: Asynchronous serial sends bits without a clock line
Both sides must agree on baud rate (9600 is common) and framing (8N1)
8N1 sends 10 bits per byte including start and stop bits
Wire TX to RX and share ground; TTL and RS-232 levels differ

resources.title: I2C
resources.description: Covers I2C signals, addressing, open-drain wiring with pull-ups, bus speeds, and how it compares to UART and SPI.
keyPoints: Two signals: SDA (data) and SCL (clock)
Messages start with an address frame; each frame is ACKed or NACKed
Open-drain lines need pull-ups, commonly 4.7 kohm
Typical speeds 100 kHz or 400 kHz; multiple controllers are possible

resources.title: Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI)
resources.description: Explains SPI's clock, data and chip-select lines, how multiple peripherals share a bus, and SPI's pros and cons.
keyPoints: Signals: SCK clock, controller-out and controller-in data lines, chip select
Chip select is active low; each peripheral usually needs its own CS line
Synchronous and faster than asynchronous serial; supports full duplex
Needs more wires and is meant for short distances

resources.title: Pull-up Resistors
resources.description: Explains floating inputs, how pull-up resistors set a default level, how to size them, and microcontroller internal pull-ups.
keyPoints: A floating input has an unpredictable state
A pull-up holds the pin high; pressing a button connects it to ground
About 10 kohm is a typical value; lower values are 'stronger'
Arduino enables internal pull-ups with pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP)

stages.title: Connecting Devices with Wi-Fi & MQTT
stages.description: Getting an ESP32 onto Wi-Fi and exchanging data through an MQTT broker using publish/subscribe, topics and QoS levels.
learningObjectives: Connect an ESP32 to a Wi-Fi network in station mode
Contrast direct client-server requests with MQTT's broker-based publish/subscribe
Design MQTT topic names and use wildcards
Choose an appropriate MQTT QoS level

explainBack.question: Several ESP32 sensors around a house must report temperatures to a dashboard that can also send commands back. Explain how they join the network and how MQTT moves the data.
rubric: In station (STA) mode the ESP32 joins an existing access point with WiFi.begin(ssid, password) and waits until WiFi.status() reports WL_CONNECTED; in AP mode other devices connect to the ESP32

With MQTT, clients connect to a broker that routes messages: publishers and subscribers do not need to know each other's IP or port or be running at the same time, unlike direct client-server requests
MQTT is lightweight (small clients and message headers suited to microcontrollers) and bidirectional, so the cloud can also send messages to devices
Topics are case-sensitive UTF-8 strings with levels separated by '/'; '+' matches one level, '#' matches all remaining levels and must be last; avoid leading slashes and spaces
QoS 0 is at most once, QoS 1 is at least once (duplicates possible), QoS 2 is exactly once via a four-step handshake; delivery uses the lower of the publisher's and subscriber's QoS

resources.title: What is MQTT | MQTT Essentials Part 1
resources.description: First episode of HiveMQ's MQTT Essentials series introducing what MQTT is and why it is used for IoT messaging.
keyPoints: Introduces MQTT and its origins
Explains why it suits constrained IoT devices
Previews publish/subscribe and the broker

resources.title: Wi-Fi API
resources.description: Official Arduino-ESP32 reference for the Wi-Fi library: station and access-point modes, connecting and checking status.
keyPoints: Station mode: the ESP32 connects to an access point
AP mode: other devices connect to the ESP32; both modes can run together
Connect with WiFi.begin(ssid, password)
Loop until WiFi.status() == WL_CONNECTED

resources.title: MQTT: The Standard for IoT Messaging
resources.description: The protocol's home page summarizing what MQTT is and its main features for IoT devices.
keyPoints: MQTT is an OASIS-standard lightweight publish/subscribe protocol
Small clients and headers suit microcontrollers and low bandwidth
Supports device-to-cloud and cloud-to-device messaging
Three QoS levels: 0 at most once, 1 at least once, 2 exactly once
Messages can be encrypted with TLS

resources.title: MQTT Publish/Subscribe Architecture (Pub/Sub) - MQTT Essentials: Part 2
resources.description: Explains the publish/subscribe pattern, the broker's role and how it differs from client-server communication.
keyPoints: Space decoupling: publishers and subscribers don't exchange IP addresses or ports
Time decoupling: they need not run at the same time
Synchronization decoupling: neither blocks while publishing or receiving
The broker filters and routes all messages

resources.title: MQTT Topics, Wildcards, & Best Practices - MQTT Essentials: Part 5
resources.description: Covers MQTT topic structure, single- and multi-level wildcards, reserved $ topics and naming best practices.
keyPoints: Topics are case-sensitive UTF-8 strings with '/' level separators
'+' replaces exactly one level; '#' matches all lower levels and must be last
$SYS topics expose broker statistics and are excluded from '#'
Avoid leading slashes and spaces; keep topics short and specific

resources.title: What is MQTT Quality of Service (QoS) 0,1, & 2? - MQTT Essentials: Part 6
resources.description: Explains MQTT's three QoS levels, their acknowledgment flows and trade-offs, and how QoS is downgraded end to end.
keyPoints: QoS 0: fire and forget, no acknowledgment
QoS 1: at least once, retried until PUBACK; duplicates possible
QoS 2: exactly once via PUBLISH, PUBREC, PUBREL, PUBCOMP
Delivered QoS is the lower of publisher's and subscriber's levels

stages.title: Robot Motion & Feedback Control
stages.description: How two-wheeled robots steer, how wheel encoders measure motion, and how closed-loop PID control holds a target.
learningObjectives: Describe how wheel speeds steer a differential-drive robot
Compute a differential-drive robot's angular velocity from its wheel speeds
Explain how a quadrature encoder measures rotation and direction
Contrast open-loop and closed-loop control and describe the P, I and D terms

explainBack.question: Your two-wheeled robot drifts when told to drive straight. Explain how its wheels steer it, how encoders measure what the wheels are doing, and how a PID loop could correct the drift.
rubric: A differential-drive robot has two independently driven wheels on a common axis: equal speeds in the same direction drive straight, equal speeds in opposite directions spin in place, and unequal speeds follow an arc
Its angular velocity is omega = (v_r - v_l) / L, where L is the distance between the wheels
A quadrature encoder outputs two signals (A and B) 90 degrees out of phase; which one leads gives the direction, and counting pulses measures how far the shaft has turned
Open-loop control sends commands without measuring the result; closed-loop control reads a sensor, computes error = setpoint - measured value, and adjusts the output at a regular interval

The proportional term reacts to the current error (too high a gain causes oscillation), the integral term accumulates error to remove steady-state error, and the derivative term responds to the error's rate of change to reduce overshoot

resources.title: What Is PID Control? | Understanding PID Control, Part 1
resources.author: Brian Douglas
resources.description: Brian Douglas introduces feedback control and the intuition behind proportional, integral and derivative terms with minimal math.
keyPoints: Explains what a controller does and why feedback is used
Builds intuition for the P, I and D paths
Frames PID as acting on present, past and predicted error

resources.title: Differential drive robot
resources.description: University lab notes describing how a differential-drive robot moves and the equations linking wheel speeds to its path.
keyPoints: Two independently driven wheels share a common axis
Same speed, same direction: straight line; opposite directions: rotate in place
Unequal speeds produce an arc around the instantaneous center of curvature
omega = (v_r - v_l) / L and R = L(v_l + v_r) / (2(v_r - v_l))

resources.title: Adventures in Science: How to Use Rotary Encoders
resources.description: SparkFun demonstrates how rotary encoders work, including quadrature direction sensing and counting rotations for robots.
keyPoints: Shows how a quadrature encoder detects direction
Counts pulses to track shaft rotation
Mentions encoders for measuring robot travel

resources.title: How to Use Rotary Encoders
resources.description: Explains quadrature encoder outputs, how to determine direction and count increments, and how encoders differ from potentiometers.
keyPoints: A and B outputs are 90 degrees out of phase
Direction comes from which channel changes first
Pulses are counted to track position in increments
Incremental encoders rotate endlessly and measure relative motion

resources.title: The PID Controller & Theory Explained
resources.description: Explains closed-loop control, setpoint, process variable and error, the role of each PID term, response metrics and tuning methods.
keyPoints: Closed-loop control reads sensors and recalculates output at a regular interval
Error is the difference between setpoint and process variable
Integral keeps growing until error is zero, removing steady-state error
Derivative responds to rate of change and reduces overshoot
Covers rise time, overshoot, settling time and Ziegler-Nichols tuning

stages.title: Robotics Software with ROS 2
stages.description: How ROS 2 splits a robot into nodes that communicate through topics, services and actions, and how to inspect them from the command line.
learningObjectives: Explain what a ROS 2 node is and how nodes form the ROS graph
Describe publishing and subscribing to topics with typed messages
Choose between topics, services and actions for a given task
Inspect a running system with ros2 command-line tools

explainBack.question: Design the software for a mobile robot with a lidar, drive motors and a 'go to the kitchen' command using ROS 2. Explain which parts are nodes and which communication type each connection uses.
rubric: Each node has a single modular purpose (e.g. driving the wheel motors or publishing laser data); one executable can contain several nodes, and nodes exchange data via topics, services, actions or parameters
Topics act as a bus: a node can publish to and subscribe to any number of topics, and publishers and subscribers must use the same message type
Services use call-and-response: a server returns data only when a client calls it, while continuous data streams belong on topics
Actions are for long-running tasks: they have a goal, feedback and a result, and can be cancelled
'ros2 topic list -t' shows topics with their message types, 'ros2 topic echo' prints live messages, and 'ros2 topic pub' publishes a YAML-formatted message from the command line

resources.title: 10 things you need to know about ROS! | Getting Ready to Build Robots with ROS #4
resources.description: A fast-paced overview of the core ROS ideas: nodes, topics, messages, services, parameters, launch files and more.
keyPoints: Introduces nodes and how they communicate
Explains topics, messages and services
Covers parameters, launch files and other core tools

resources.title: ROS Overview
resources.description: Written companion to the video summarizing nodes, topics, messages, services, parameters, launch files and ROS distributions.
keyPoints: Each program in a ROS system is a node
A topic is a named location nodes publish messages to; subscribers receive them
Services are a single request/reply between two nodes
Launch files start and configure groups of nodes
New ROS distributions are released each May

resources.title: Understanding nodes
resources.description: Official ROS 2 tutorial explaining nodes, the ROS graph, and how to run and list nodes from the command line.
keyPoints: The ROS graph is the network of elements processing data together
Each node should have a single, modular purpose
Nodes communicate via topics, services, actions or parameters
One executable can contain one or more nodes

resources.title: Understanding topics
resources.description: Official tutorial on topics as the bus between nodes, with ros2 topic commands for listing, echoing and publishing messages.
keyPoints: Topics act as a bus for nodes to exchange messages
A node can publish and subscribe to any number of topics
'ros2 topic list -t' adds message types; the type is how nodes agree on data
'ros2 topic echo' shows live data; 'ros2 topic pub' sends YAML messages

resources.title: Understanding services
resources.description: Official tutorial contrasting call-and-response services with topics and showing how to list and call services.
keyPoints: Services use call-and-response instead of publish/subscribe
Topics give continual updates; services return data only when called
A service has a request and a response structure

resources.title: Understanding actions
resources.description: Official tutorial on actions for long-running tasks: goals, feedback, results and cancellation.
keyPoints: Actions are intended for long-running tasks
They consist of a goal, feedback and a result
Unlike services, actions are cancelable and give steady feedback

stages.title: IoT Security & Power
stages.description: Baseline security for connected devices (credentials, updates, encryption) and stretching battery life with power budgets and sleep modes.
learningObjectives: Apply baseline consumer-IoT security practices for credentials and exposed services
Secure device communication with TLS
Explain how safe over-the-air (OTA) firmware updates work
Estimate battery life and use microcontroller sleep modes to extend it

explainBack.question: You are shipping 50 battery-powered ESP32 sensors that report over MQTT. Explain the security measures you would build in and how you would make the batteries last.
rubric: Devices must not use universal default passwords, credentials must not be hard-coded in firmware, and unused ports/services should be closed (least privilege)
Software must be securely updatable; ESP-IDF OTA writes the new image to the inactive app slot (ota_0/ota_1) and can roll back if the new firmware fails its self-check
TLS encrypts MQTT traffic and protects it from alteration; plain MQTT uses port 1883 and MQTT over TLS uses 8883, and the server certificate should be validated
Battery life is roughly capacity (mAh) divided by average current (mA), e.g. 2000 mAh / 100 mA = about 20 hours, so cutting average current extends runtime

ESP32 deep sleep powers off the CPUs, most RAM and digital peripherals, keeping only RTC parts; it wakes on a timer, GPIO or touch, restarts like a reset (RTC memory can keep data), and Wi-Fi connections are not maintained

resources.title: Wakeup From Sleep With a Timer (ESP32 + Arduino series)
resources.description: Shows how to put an ESP32 into deep sleep and wake it on a timer from the Arduino environment to save power.
keyPoints: Puts an ESP32 into deep sleep
Configures a timer wake-up source
Shows how the program restarts after waking

resources.title: Code of Practice for Consumer IoT Security
resources.description: Thirteen government guidelines for securing consumer connected devices, from banning default passwords to validating input.
keyPoints: No universal default passwords; each device password must be unique
Software should be securely updateable with a published support period
Hard-coded credentials in device software are not acceptable
Encrypt security-sensitive data in transit
Apply least privilege and close unused ports

resources.title: TLS/SSL - MQTT Security Fundamentals
resources.description: Explains how TLS secures MQTT connections, the standard ports, certificate validation and options for constrained devices.
keyPoints: TLS stops third parties reading or altering traffic
MQTT uses port 1883; MQTT over TLS uses 8883
The TLS handshake costs a few kilobytes, small for long-lived connections
Validate X.509 certificates to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks

resources.title: Over The Air Updates (OTA)
resources.description: Official ESP-IDF documentation of the OTA partition scheme, rollback and anti-rollback, and signed firmware.
keyPoints: Needs at least two app slots (ota_0, ota_1) plus an OTA data partition
New firmware is written to the slot that is not running
App rollback reverts if the new image is not marked valid after self-tests
Anti-rollback blocks older, less secure versions; images can be signed

resources.title: Battery Technologies
resources.description: Explains battery capacity, estimating runtime, and the characteristics and safe handling of common chemistries such as LiPo and NiMH.
keyPoints: Capacity is commonly rated in milliamp-hours (mAh)
Runtime is roughly capacity divided by current draw
A LiPo cell is 3.7 V nominal and needs a dedicated charger
Many LiPo cells have protection circuits against over-discharge

resources.title: Sleep Modes
resources.description: Official ESP32 documentation of light sleep and deep sleep, what stays powered, wake-up sources and Wi-Fi behavior.
keyPoints: Light sleep clock-gates CPUs and RAM; state is kept
Deep sleep powers off CPUs, most RAM and digital peripherals; RTC parts stay on
Wake sources include timer, EXT0/EXT1 GPIO, touch and ULP
Waking from deep sleep restarts like a reset; RTC memory can retain data
Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connections are not kept during sleep

name: IoT & Robot Automation
description: Build connected devices and simple robots: circuits, microcontrollers, sensors and motors, bus protocols, MQTT, motion control, ROS 2, and secure low-power design.
